A SMALL GUIDE TO BIG MEMORY BLANKS

10 tips to
memorize
kanji.

Staring until they stare back
still isn't a study method.

Ridiculous stories, useful details and reviews that do something. Give your brain a job and it has more to work with.

By Kanjidon Team · Japanese, one piece at a time

You studied a kanji. You recognized it. You were practically on speaking terms. The next day, it's a complete stranger with a flair for geometry.

To memorize kanji, try linking the shape to a meaning, learning it in a word and recalling it without looking. Then come back to it after a break. These ten tips turn that idea into something you can actually do, without filling your home with guilt.

PICK YOUR STARTING POINT

01 · Pieces02 · Stories03 · Words04 · Recall05 · Review06 · Lookalikes07 · Pencil08 · The hunt09 · Kanjidon10 · Routine
01

TAKE THE MONSTER APART

Look at the pieces,
not the tangle.

A new kanji can look like the aftermath of a toothpick fight. Look for shapes you already know. In 休, you'll find 亻, a form of “person”, and 木, “tree”. Two footholds are easier to work with than six unrelated strokes.

Try this: choose three kanji and spot a recurring component. You don't need to memorize the entire radical catalogue before you're allowed to start.

A quick distinction: components are the pieces you can see; the radical is the one used to classify a character in a dictionary. They aren't always the same thing.
Explore radicals and components ↗

A BOTANICAL BREAK

The woods were in the character all along.

木 is a tree. You can spot two in 林 and three in 森. A little visual family for tree, grove and forest. Not every kanji gives up its meaning this easily. These ones are being helpful for a change.

林 on Kanjipedia ↗
木ki · tree
林hayashi · grove
森mori · forest
02

THE SCREENWRITING DEPARTMENT

Make up a story.
A silly one is fine.

For 休, “rest”, picture someone leaning against a tree with their phone set to “not today”. The scene ties the pieces to the meaning. If it sticks, it's done its job.

Try this: one scene, using the components that are actually there. Cover the meaning and see if you can recall it. If you remember the entire sitcom but not the kanji, shorten the script.

A mnemonic story is your own memory aid. It isn't automatically the character's etymology, and it won't teach you the pronunciation on its own.

03

WORDS DON'T LIVE IN BOXES

Learn a word,
not a list of readings.

Instead of chasing every reading of 山 at once, start with 山 (やま, yama, mountain). Then meet it in 火山 (かざん, kazan, volcano). Same character, different reading in a real word. Context finally gets a speaking part.

山yama mountain→火山kazan volcano

Try this: choose a common word for each new kanji, listen to a reliable pronunciation and repeat it. Add other readings as you encounter them. No need to adopt the whole family on day one.

04

TAKE OFF THE TRAINING WHEELS

Cover the answer.
Let your brain do the work.

Rereading “mountain, mountain, mountain” can feel reassuringly familiar. Instead, look at 山 and say its meaning before revealing the answer. That's a small retrieval practice exercise.

Try this: five cards, answers hidden, one honest attempt. Check straight away. If you get one wrong, find the detail you missed and try again after a few other cards. A wrong answer tells you where to focus.

Retrieval practice and spreading study over time have strong support in learning research. They don't make memory infallible, but they give review a clear purpose.

A TINY QUIZ WITH NO GRADES

You've met this character.
What do you remember?

Try saying its meaning and a word before opening the answer.

山
Let's check

Mountain. On its own: やま, yama. In 火山, kazan, it joins 火 to form “volcano”. Drew a blank? Check, then try again later.

05

THE SECOND MEETING MATTERS

Meet it again tomorrow.
Then give it some space.

Ten encounters in one evening aren't ten encounters spread over time. Spaced repetition organizes your return visits: try to remember, check, then meet the material in another session.

Try this: after studying something new, test yourself the next day and again a few days later. If recall holds up, widen the gap; if it wobbles, return sooner. It's an example to adapt, not a sacred calendar carved into Mount Fuji. An SRS can help manage the intervals.

Make spaced repetition work for you ↗
06

THE ALMOST-IDENTICAL CLUB

One picks up.
The other throws away.

拾う (hirou) means “pick up”; 捨てる (suteru) means “throw away”. They look alike, but with the last cookie at stake, you want to be clear.

Both have 扌, the hand component, on the left. Look right: 拾 contains 合; 捨 contains 舎, with a vertical stroke in the middle above the little square 口. That's where to focus your eyes.

拾pick up
hirou · 拾う
捨throw away
suteru · 捨てる

Try this: study the pair, then cover the explanations. Which one would you use for picking up a coin? Which for throwing away a receipt? Swap their order and try again. Recognize the character, not where it was sitting.

Train your eye with more kanji lookalikes ↗
峠

A LITTLE UPHILL CURIOSITY

A kanji with built-in navigation.

峠 (とうげ, tōge) means a mountain pass. It's a kokuji, a character created in Japan, combining mountain 山, up 上 and down 下. Here, the journey really is part of the character's formation. The blisters are your contribution.

The story of 峠 on Kanjipedia ↗
07

YOUR PENCIL ISN'T A PHOTOCOPIER

Write it once while looking.
Then try without.

Copying a character twenty times can keep your hand busy while your brain takes a holiday. Instead, study a reliable model and its stroke order, reproduce it carefully, cover it and try to rebuild it.

Try this: compare your attempt with the model. Missing a stroke? Changed a proportion? Fix that specific detail. If reading is your main goal, use writing as a targeted aid and leave time for recognizing kanji in words too.

08

LET THEM OUT OF YOUR NOTEBOOK

Hunt down a kanji.
In a real sentence.

Pick a character you've just studied and look for it in an easy text, a menu or a sentence at your level. Found 山 in 山に行きます。 (やまにいきます, “I'm going to the mountains”)? Good. It's doing something besides occupying a box.

Try this: save a short sentence, check its reading and meaning, and reread it tomorrow. One sentence you understand beats a manga page decoded with three dictionaries and a search-and-rescue team.

09

A GOOD REASON TO COME BACK

Download Kanjidon.
The card starts it. Review makes it count.

Did we put ourselves on the list? Yes. With a responsibility: to make you want to study and give you something concrete to do. In Kanjidon, kanji become cards to discover in packs and collect, with quizzes and spaced repetition to practice recall.

Try this: choose a kanji you're studying, try a quiz and come back to your reviews. Collecting is fun. Remembering what you've collected is the part you'll use outside the app.

For iPhone and Android. Features and access depend on your plan.
The game brings you back. Review helps the kanji stay.

10

SMALL IS A GREAT SIZE

Build a routine
that fits your life.

“Fifty kanji a day, starting Monday” is a wonderful title for a project that stops answering emails by Thursday. Choose a manageable amount, including reviews.

Try this: attach a short session to something already in your day, like finishing breakfast. Start with reviews, then add a few new items. If the backlog grows, cut back on new material. Miss a day? Start again. No kanji will demand a written apology.

START HERE TODAY

Three kanji. One small mission.

  1. Look at the pieces. Choose three characters at your level and a word for each.
  2. Try without help. Cover meaning and reading, answer, then check.
  3. Plan the next meeting. Try again tomorrow and adjust your reviews.

You don't have to use all ten tips at once.
The best method is one you can actually put into practice.

THE QUESTIONS THAT ALWAYS COME UP

Before your brain
opens another tab.

How many kanji should I study each day?

There's no right number for everyone. Try starting with three new characters and see how reviews go over the next few days. If the workload grows too much, reduce new material. Three is a starting experiment, not a scientific threshold.

Do I need to learn every reading straight away?

No. Start with the words you're using: meaning, reading and context. Add other readings as you encounter new vocabulary. A dictionary helps you look things up; it doesn't set tonight's learning quota.

Are little stories enough to remember kanji?

They can help create an initial connection, but you need to test it. Recall the meaning without help, check the answer and find the character in words. If a story doesn't help, change it or drop it.

Why do I forget kanji I've already studied?

Seeing them before doesn't guarantee you can always recall them. Check whether you're only rereading, leaving too long between reviews or confusing similar shapes. A blank tells you what to revisit, not how talented you are at Japanese.
